title: Writing OpenAPI Specifications
learning_outcomes: Explain how writing openapi specifications affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from yaml and json formats to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on writing openapi specifications in api contracts and documentation. You will connect yaml and json formats to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Writing OpenAPI Specifications matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying yaml and json formats deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 139 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 139: YAML and JSON formats → Operation IDs, tags, and summaries → Request and response schemas → Required, nullable, and optional fields.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: An OpenAPI description is a machine-readable contract; it should match implemented methods, schemas, security, and errors. In this lesson, treat “Writing OpenAPI Specifications” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Writing OpenAPI Specifications
content_blocks.code:
openapi: 3.1.2
info:
  title: Task API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /v1/tasks:
    get:
      operationId: listTasks
      responses:
        "200":
          description: A bounded page of tasks
content_blocks.expected_output: This compact OpenAPI fragment describes an operation and a response contract. Validate the full document with tooling compatible with the declared OpenAPI version.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “YAML and JSON formats”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Operation IDs, tags, and summaries” and “Required, nullable, and optional fields”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: The contract should explain successful requests, failures, authentication, schemas, and compatibility. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating writing openapi specifications. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “YAML and JSON formats” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Writing OpenAPI Specifications with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating writing openapi specifications as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: An OpenAPI description is a machine-readable contract; it should match implemented methods, schemas, security, and errors. In this lesson, treat “Writing OpenAPI Specifications” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 140: Documenting Authentication and Errors.
